title: POLONIUM
summary: POLONIUM is a Lebanon linked espionage cluster that public reporting describes as focused on Israel and the wider Middle East, with targeting across critical infrastructure, healthcare, insurance, technology and government. Its distinguishing feature is supply chain access: instead of attacking every victim directly, reporting describes compromise of managed service providers and information technology consultancies so that one successful intrusion yields many downstream victims. Tradecraft includes custom lightweight implants, abuse of legitimate cloud storage services for command and control, and the reuse of remote management software already present in the victim environment. Because command and control rides on trusted cloud endpoints and administrative tools, network detection depends on behavioural context rather than blocklists: unusual processes uploading to cloud storage, management agents running outside maintenance windows, and authentication from an internet service provider that does not match the account's normal pattern. The frequent misunderstanding is that supply chain risk means third party software: here it is third party people and access, which defensive contracts, least privilege and monitoring of provider accounts must address. Public research associates the activity with a state interest at moderate confidence, and the cluster name covers a set of observed behaviours.

beginner.definition: POLONIUM is a research name for a group that spies on organisations in the Middle East, especially in Israel. Instead of attacking each victim directly, it often breaks into the technology companies that support them. Those companies then become an easier path to many targets at once.
beginner.whyItMatters: Almost every company relies on outside providers for email, networks and support. If an attacker takes over one provider, they can reach all of that provider's customers. That is far more efficient than attacking each customer separately, and it is much harder for the customers to see. The group also hides its traffic inside normal cloud services, so simple blocking rules will not work. Trust in your providers must be managed, not assumed.
howItWorks: The group studies which technology providers support the organisations it wants to reach.
It compromises a provider, then uses that provider's trusted access to enter customer networks.
Inside, it installs small tools and reuses remote management software that is already present.
It sends instructions through ordinary cloud storage services, so the traffic looks normal.
It collects documents and credentials slowly, staying below the level that triggers alerts.
It keeps the access alive for a long time by adding accounts and renewing its tools.
beginner.example: Think of a hotel that hires one cleaning company for all its rooms. The cleaning staff hold master keys and come and go without suspicion. A thief who gets hired by that cleaning company does not need to break any hotel door. He walks in with the cleaners, enters any room, and takes what he likes. The hotel trusted the cleaner, not the room. That is supply chain risk. The weakest point was never the locked door, it was the trusted person holding the key.
takeaways: Give outside providers only the access they need, and review that access regularly.
Watch for administration tools and cloud uploads happening at unusual times.
Public reporting links this cluster to a state interest with moderate confidence.

objectives: Explain how compromising a service provider grants access to many downstream customers at once.
Describe why legitimate cloud services used for command and control defeat simple domain and address blocklists.
Identify the detection opportunities in provider accounts, remote management agents and cloud storage activity.
Apply least privilege and contractual controls to reduce third party access risk in a supply chain.
Summarise the targeting and attribution described in public reporting for this cluster.
